Civil and business contracts are presumed equal and symmetrical until there are concrete elements that justify setting this presumption aside, subject to the legal regimes provided for in special laws, it also being guaranteed that: I - the negotiating parties may establish objective parameters for the interpretation of the contractual clauses and of their grounds for revision or termination; II - the allocation of risks defined by the parties must be respected and observed; and III - contractual revision shall only occur in an exceptional and limited manner.

Whoever sells, works or builds a clientele on a platform without being a consumer is still protected by the Civil Code, with a greater demand for proof.
1. What you built on a platform is an asset, even without a body.
2. Whoever sells in an online store, works through an app or builds a client network inside another company's system can also lose what they built.
3. You have the asset, but you do not control the conditions for using what you have, and that is where the problem lies.

The word on the button is not there by chance. In everyday Portuguese, and in the Civil Code too, to buy is to exchange money for a thing that becomes yours. Whoever buys expects the thing to stay, not to disappear without reason and to be good for something. This holds even when you know the item is digital, because the word raises that expectation on its own, like a shortcut the mind takes without thinking.

What you bought exists and has value, but it can only be used on the inside of a turnstile, like those at a subway station, and the platform controls the turnstile. It decides who gets through, who stays and on what conditions, both by contract and by technology.

And what you bought does not stop existing just because you cannot hold it in your hand. The company itself defines in the contract what virtual content is, names the items and links them to your account. It also admits that you can obtain this content by buying it, earning it in missions or receiving it as a gift. In doing so, it recognises that there is an identifiable set of things there, and that recognition dismantles the idea that nothing was delivered.

With all of this together, it becomes clear why the expression revocable licence deserves suspicion. It gives the impression that nothing was delivered and that everything can disappear without consequence. But if there is an identifiable item, linked to your account and used in the game, there is something the law must take seriously. And that holds even if the contract speaks of it in the language of something precarious.

And not every annoyance becomes a right. This category does not serve to turn any discomfort of digital use into a loss the law repairs, nor to condemn every technical choice of the company. An update, a change on the screen or a new order in the game's lists are not unlawful in themselves. What counts is serious and lasting deterioration, recognisable by criteria, that hits the core of what was sold, even when access continues.
This also means that nothing here decides a case on its own. The tools exist, but each conflict still depends on what happened, on what can be proved and on how the decision-maker reads the facts.

Nor is it about opening the game's code or handing over the company's secrets. What is asked is a demonstrable minimum, enough to see whether there was a relevant change, link it to what was promised and check whether it had a justification. It is sufficient transparency, not total transparency.

When the platform changes something important in your access, in the item's performance, in its usefulness or in the rules of the game, or when it applies a punishment. And it does so without keeping the minimum record needed to reconstruct what happened. This is the case of the item that loses strength in an update without a verifiable explanation, or of the account suspended without anyone knowing on what basis.
The test compares the item's role, not only whether it is still in the account
<1></1><2>What it was worth at purchase</2><3>What was left after the change</3>

<1>What the item does</1><2><3>What it was worth at purchase. </3>It works and fulfils the use you paid for</2><4><5>What was left after the change. </5>It still opens, but lost the function that justified the purchase</4>

<1>The relationship with others</1><2><3>What it was worth at purchase. </3>It marks your place and is recognised by those who play with you</2><4><5>What was left after the change. </5>It became common, downgraded or out of the place it held</4>
<1>What it means</1><2><3>What it was worth at purchase. </3>It carries distinction, history or belonging</2><4><5>What was left after the change. </5>It lost the meaning that made it yours</4>
None of this requires freezing the service. The test asks that the item's role be preserved in essence, not that nothing change. <1><2>p. 729-730</2></1>

None of this becomes an automatic formula. The path only organises questions. What form of platform governance is at stake? What duty was breached? What minimum proof can be required? How does the case qualify in law? And what response makes sense for it?

What unites these cases is not the economic sector or the type of technology. It is the way the platform governs use, manages what you expect, controls what can be understood and makes challenging easier or harder.
The question is always the same, anywhere. Is it possible to know what was promised and what changed? And is it possible to react?

The rank does not order you to play more. It is you who wants to climb. Behind the visible rank there is a secret number that measures you, and the company says the rank serves precisely to translate that number into a form that can be followed. What you see is the position, and the calculation stays hidden.

What is asked is proportional to the power the company exercises. Transparency that serves a purpose, a minimum of stability, verifiable reasons, a real way to challenge and the restoration of what was lost.
The platform must follow understandable procedures, give a reason that can be checked, let you challenge reasonably and not treat you arbitrarily.

If the punishment has no verifiable reason or reasonable way to challenge it, its review or reversal may be due. You can also ask the platform to fulfil procedural duties and to create or improve a real way to challenge. When the problem repeats with many people, it is also possible to ask that the punishment system as a whole be corrected.

The platform has the power to punish, but having that power is not enough. The punishment needs a verifiable reason, consistency from one decision to the next and an understandable way to challenge it.

A skin changes the character's look, effects and animations, and does so again in every match. Some people put a lot of money, many hours and much attention into it. Seen from outside, it seems excessive to pay a lot for an outfit that does not exist off the screen.

The things we consume work like signs, some saying welcome and others saying keep out. It is through them that people align with some, set themselves apart from others and give meaning to what they live. The skin does this inside the game, because it shows which group you belong to and who does not belong to it.

In a piece of music, a single note says almost nothing, because the music lies in the relation between the notes. Something similar happens with the things we consume. An isolated skin says little, because its meaning comes from the place it occupies beside the others, from what is common and what is rare.

The spectacle is not a heap of images, but people relating to each other through images. In a match, your skin is seen, compared and commented on, and its value is made in this scene that never stops.

Absence stops being a pause and becomes a measurable fall. And the risk lies not only in the item, but in the meaning of what is lost and in the calendar, which turns delay into disadvantage, even when the skin is still there, technically accessible.

You can ask that the offer be corrected and fulfilled, that what you lost be restored and that the misleading communication stop. In some cases, it is possible to ask that sales strategies incompatible with what is actually delivered be struck down. Depending on the case, the law may treat this as misleading or abusive advertising, or as an offer that binds whoever advertised it.

And there are legitimate purposes the platform can and should pursue, such as security, stability and game balance. The abusive purpose only appears when it can be shown, with reasons, that the design points mainly to exploiting your fragility and capturing value disproportionately, and not to those ends.
We are used to looking for abuse in a contract clause, in a sentence that can be underlined. But sometimes no single clause is the problem.

What is asked, in the end, are criteria already known. Information that is truly understood, respect for trust, equivalence of what was bought, changes that leave a trace, a real possibility of undoing what was done and a minimum chance to challenge. When the design starts working against these criteria, the service itself becomes an instrument of exploitation.

In serious cases, losing the account, the history or the trajectory can affect your personality and give rise to moral damages. This happens when the loss demonstrably hits your history, your belonging or the reputation and memory you built inside.
Not every way of selling, persuading or running the game is abusive. What is controlled is a programme recognisable in how the environment works, and not someone's hidden will.

It all began with a simple question, whether the skin is yours. Along the way, a kind of consumption appeared in which you imagine you are standing on your own ground, but you only walk on borrowed ground, which can be taken away and remade at any moment.
